messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 64
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 60

# The Weight of Locked Doors

Ranjit is a 64-year-old South Asian man who has worked in a large distribution warehouse on the outskirts of the city for the past eleven years. He lives with his wife, Meena, in a modest home they have shared for over three decades. To his coworkers, he is the quiet one — dependable, methodical, always the first to arrive and the last to complain. What they do not know is that Ranjit has not slept through a single night in more than two years.

Twenty-six months ago, Ranjit was traveling alone to visit relatives in his home country when he was abducted by a criminal group and held for ransom. He was kept in a series of small, dark rooms — sometimes a concrete cell, sometimes a locked shed — for forty-one days. He was bound for long stretches, given minimal food and water, and subjected to repeated threats on his life. His captors spoke to him in ways designed to make him believe he would never be found. There were moments, he says quietly, when he believed them.

He was eventually released following negotiations he was never fully informed of. He returned home physically weakened and, in his own words, "not the same man who left."

In the months that followed, Ranjit tried to resume his life. He returned to the warehouse, lifting boxes and operating the forklift along the same routes he had walked for years. But the warehouse, with its long corridors, its heavy rolling doors, and its windowless loading bays, began to feel unbearable in ways he could not immediately name. He found himself mapping exits the moment he arrived each shift. When a colleague accidentally locked a storage room with Ranjit inside — for less than three minutes — Ranjit's body responded as though the forty-one days had returned all at once. He could not speak for the rest of the afternoon.

At home, Meena watches him the way one watches something fragile. He no longer sleeps in their bedroom. He tells her it is because he does not want to disturb her with his restlessness, but the truth is that the darkness of the room closes in on him in ways he cannot control. He sleeps in the living room with the television on and the hallway light burning. Even so, he wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart hammering, certain he can smell the damp concrete of the shed where he spent his longest stretch of captivity.

He rarely speaks of what happened. In his culture, in his generation, men are expected to absorb suffering privately, and Ranjit has tried to honor that expectation. But the effort of containment is visible in everything he does. He has stopped attending the temple he visited every week for thirty years because the enclosed prayer hall triggers a tightening in his chest he cannot manage in public. He has declined every family gathering held indoors. He does not take the subway. He has not been on an airplane.

His appetite is poor. He has lost nearly fifteen pounds. Meena prepares the foods he has always loved, and he eats small portions to spare her feelings. He tells her he is fine. He tells himself the same thing, with less conviction each time.

What troubles Ranjit most is not the fear itself — he has made a kind of uneasy peace with the idea that fear will accompany him now — but the shame of it. He is sixty-four years old. He survived. He came home. He watches younger men at the warehouse move through their days with an ease that feels almost incomprehensible to him now, and he wonders, with a grief he cannot quite articulate, what happened to the person he used to be — the man who left for that trip without a second thought, who locked his own front door behind him and never once considered what it might feel like to be on the wrong side of one.
